examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/d0cebdd804ff244d037e14df6ec33efb86b522644f7b4addc688e27fd6a57e95.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} y^3e^{-x} \: \textrm{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x = \ln{y}$ from $(0, 1)$ to $\left(\dfrac32\ln 2 , 2\sqrt{2}\right),$ as shown above.
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x = x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x = x(t) = \ln{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \ln{t}, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints on the path.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{|t|} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y) = y^3e^{-x},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t} \\  & ={t}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{3}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u = t^2 + 1,$ $\textrm{d}u = 2t \, \textrm{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{2}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\sqrt{{9}^{3}}-\sqrt{{2}^{3}}] \\  & =\frac{27-2\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/6cabe5598368b4f26ccca515d4f4011100e0bc410b72d919db9681b3145814fb.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ traversed between the points $(0,1)$ and $(2,{e}^{2}),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le {e}^{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le {e}^{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{|t|} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)={e}^{x}{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}){t}^{2} \\  & =(t){t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{t}^{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
